summary.field_subfield: Supramolecular chemistry / biomaterials (bioinspired interfaces for regenerative medicine and drug delivery)
summary.executive_summary: This Feature Article reviews recent work on bioinspired supramolecular materials that mimic the dynamic contact events occurring at biological interfaces between and within cells. The authors argue that cellular activities such as adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation are driven by dynamic biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies including extracellular matrices, phospholipid bilayers, and membrane proteins, and that mimicking these dynamic actions is an effective route to biomaterials for regenerative medicine and drug delivery. The article highlights two material classes: artificial extracellular matrices built from self-assembling peptide hydrogels, and membrane-deforming supramolecular materials. For the ECM class, the authors describe stiffness-controlled supramolecular peptide hydrogels based on RADA16 and its glycine mutants A16G and A8G, showing that fibre morphology tunes hydrogel stiffness and that A16G-N-cadherin conjugates markedly enhance neuroblast migration in an injured neonatal neocortex in vivo. They also describe JigSAP fibre-forming peptides with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces that efficiently incorporate and sustain-release full-length proteins such as VEGF, promoting angiogenesis in an ischaemic stroke mouse model. For kinetics control, redox-responsive peptides bearing methionine residues undergo gel-to-sol transitions upon oxidation by hydrogen peroxide, enabling stimulus-controlled cargo release. For the membrane class, the authors describe highly stable phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) stabilized by a cholic acid–metal-binding-peptide surfactant crosslinked with copper ions, which show prolonged blood circulation relative to spherical vesicles. Finally, they describe an amphiphilic molecular machine (AzoMEx) that undergoes light-triggered opening/closing motion to expand a giant unilamellar vesicle membrane and induce endocytosis-like fission, enabling efficient encapsulation of micrometer-size M13 phage viruses and their delivery to multiple organs via blood administration. The authors conclude that these supramolecular approaches to mimicking and controlling bio-interfaces present powerful ways to develop regenerative medicines and drug delivery systems, while noting that the materials science of reconstructing biomimetic dynamic interfaces is still in its infancy. The article is a review rather than an empirical study, so it reports no participant sample size, no numerical sample, and no statistical metrics; accordingly, fields that require reported data or code are set to empty strings. The narrative is grounded in verbatim fragments from the text, including specific incorporation percentages, release percentages, stiffness values, dilution conditions, and organ infectivity values, which are preserved with all key numbers.

Research Context
Cellular activities depend on dynamic bio-interfaces. Bio-interfaces include ECM, phospholipid bilayers, and membrane proteins. Key dynamic functions are adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transport. ECM regulates migration and releases signaling factors. Phospholipid bilayer deformation drives exo- and endocytosis. Supramolecular chemistry enables dynamic bio-interface materials. Such materials can support regenerative medicine and drug delivery. Brain neuron regeneration is limited and hard to treat. Bicelles are unstable and prone to phase transitions. Endocytosis-like transport by molecular machines is unexplored.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can self-assembling peptide hydrogels mimic ECM to guide neuron migration? Can fibre morphology tune hydrogel stiffness? Does A16G-N-cadherin enhance neuroblast migration in vivo? Can peptide fibres incorporate and release full-length proteins? Does JigSAP promote angiogenesis in stroke models? Can redox-responsive peptides control cargo release kinetics? Can peptide-stabilized nanosheets enable extended blood circulation? Can a molecular machine enable endocytosis-like viral delivery? The authors hypothesized that combining dynamic peptide properties with protein display and sustained release would enable neuronal migration and neural tissue regeneration. The authors hypothesized that copper-mediated crosslinking would stabilize nanosheets for prolonged circulation. The authors hypothesized that light-triggered membrane expansion would allow efficient encapsulation of large viruses.

Methodological Details
This is a Feature Article reviewing recent studies rather than an original empirical dataset. The review covers artificial ECMs and membrane-deforming materials. Peptide amphiphiles form nanofibres via cylindrical micelles. Diphenylalanine is used as a fibre backbone. RADA16 peptides form nanofibres via hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions. Glycine residues enhance conformational flexibility of polypeptide chains. A8G is a mutant of RADA16 with central alanine replaced by glycine. A16G is a mutant of RADA16 with terminal alanine replaced by glycine. N-cadherin guides neuroblast migration along radial glial fibres. Dcx is a marker for neuroblasts.

Procedures And Architectures
Time-lapse imaging was used to assess neuroblast migration on hydrogels. In vivo injection was performed into an injured neonatal neocortex. JigSAP has a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface enabling protein incorporation. JigSAP sequence is Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2. AXXXA and GXXXG motifs drive α-helix-to-β-strand transitions. MD simulation was used to calculate JigSAP self-assembly. CD spectroscopy tracked helical-to-β-sheet conversion over 100 hours. JigSAP nanofibres have an average width of 3.2 nm. Rheological analysis measured storage and loss moduli versus shear strain. Incorporation efficiency was measured for EGFP and its peptide-tagged variants. Redox-responsive peptides use methionine for gel-sol control. Met is oxidized to methionine sulfoxide by reactive oxygen species.

Key Results
A16G forms bundled nanofibres and a more robust hydrogel than RADA16. A16G hydrogel shows lower stiffness than RADA16. A16G hydrogel exhibits thixotropic properties. Neuroblast migration rate was significantly higher with A16G-N-cadherin than A16G alone. Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed with A16G-A16G-Ncad mixture in vivo. Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Fibre morphology affects macroscopic hydrogel properties. A16G hydrogel combining enhanced mobility with decreased stiffness is advantageous for injection. A16G-N-cadherin mimics intrinsic scaffold cells for neuro-regenerative therapy. JigSAP enables controlled sustained release of full-length growth factors. Redox-responsive peptides allow kinetics-controlled cargo release. Copper-mediated crosslinking stabilizes nanosheets for prolonged circulation. Nanosheets enable prolonged circulation relative to spherical vesicles. AzoMEx enables endocytosis-like outside-in membrane deformation. Encapsulated viruses retain infectivity across multiple organs. These approaches enable encapsulation and delivery of biomacromolecules.

Contradictions And Limitations
The article is a Feature Article review, not an original empirical dataset. The review cites prior studies but does not provide primary experimental data. The materials science of reconstructing biomimetic dynamic interfaces is still in its infancy. The review notes the field is expected to make significant progress in the future.
